title: Catholic: the rosary
hook: beads, prayers, and the stories of Jesus and Mary, one decade at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Eucharist, and the red lamp that never goes out. Your line was real presence. Who got your full attention? Day two hundred sixty-one.

Maybe you've seen one hanging from a rearview mirror. Or wrapped around a grandmother's fingers in a hospital waiting room, her lips moving without a sound. Or laid in the hands of someone at a funeral. A loop of beads with a small cross at the end. It looks like jewelry, but anyone who uses it will tell you it's something you do, not something you wear. Its rhythm has carried people through long nights, long drives and long grief. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the rosary.
screen: `A REARVIEW MIRROR.` → `A GRANDMOTHER'S FINGERS.` → `SOMETHING YOU DO, NOT WEAR.`

segments.voice: The word comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers offered like roses. Here's how it works. The beads are grouped in tens, called decades, usually five on a rosary. Each decade begins on a single bead with the Our Father, the prayer we met last week. Then ten Hail Marys, one per bead, a prayer we'll open properly in a few days. Then a short Glory Be. And while the fingers move and the lips repeat, the mind is somewhere else: in a story. Each decade is paired with a scene from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called a mystery. The joyful mysteries include the angel's visit to Mary and the birth in Bethlehem. The sorrowful mysteries walk through the arrest and the crucifixion. The glorious mysteries begin with the resurrection. In 2002, Pope John Paul the Second added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus' public life, like his baptism and the Last Supper. So the rosary is really two things at once: a repetition for the body and a meditation for the mind. The beads keep count, so you don't have to. Where did it come from? A popular tradition says Mary gave it to Saint Dominic in the thirteenth century. Historians mostly see it growing more gradually, out of medieval monks praying the hundred and fifty psalms, and laypeople who couldn't read saying a hundred and fifty short prayers instead. Popes have recommended it ever since, and the shape has barely changed in five hundred years.
screen: `ROSARIUM — A ROSE GARDEN.` · `DECADES: ONE OUR FATHER, TEN HAIL MARYS.` · `EACH DECADE, A MYSTERY TO PONDER.` · `REPETITION FOR THE BODY, STORY FOR THE MIND.` · then, large: `ONE BEAD AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you have beads, hold them. If not, a string with ten knots, or simply your ten fingers. Move through them slowly, one breath per bead. If you pray, you can say a prayer you know on each one; if not, let each breath be a quiet thank-you. Let your mind rest on one scene, a birth, a table, a sunrise. One bead at a time. The bell holds the time.
Rosary. From rosarium, a rose garden: beads counted in decades, each one carrying a story of Jesus and Mary. Today's word.
Your line: one bead at a time. Today, when something feels too big, do only the next small piece, and then the next. Day two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the rosary daily or weekly, alone or in groups, often praying one set of mysteries assigned to each day of the week; October is traditionally the month of the rosary.
